Hi Mark. Last class you learned what to leave out of a sentence. Today you learn what to let in, and what you let in is the other side. Here is the idea. A review that only praises is an advertisement, and a review that only complains is a rant. The sentence that does both things at once is the concessive clause, and English has one for every situation. The first family is although, even though and though, and all three take a full clause after them. Although the world is stunning, the missions are repetitive. Even though I complained for an hour, I played it again on Sunday. The second family is despite and in spite of, and this is where almost every Brazilian student loses a mark. Despite does not take a clause. It takes a noun, despite the clunky menus. It takes an ing form, despite being clunky. Or it takes the fact that, despite the fact that the menus are clunky. Never despite the menus are clunky. The third family is while and whereas, and those two put things side by side without either one winning. The world is enormous, whereas the story is thin. Then there are two small ones worth having. No matter how, and however plus an adjective, for the concession that holds whatever happens. No matter how many patches they release, the ending falls flat. And though on its own, at the very end of a sentence, which is the most spoken one of all. It is worth the money, though. Now the trap that costs the most. In Portuguese you say embora and then later you say mas. In English you get one connector and only one. Although it is clunky, it is worth it. Never although it is clunky, but it is worth it. Before class, write four sentences about something you like and criticize at the same time, and use a different connector in every one. See you in class, Mark.

So that is forty hours, and here is where I have landed. Deep Harbor is the most beautiful thing I have played this year and one of the most frustrating, and I do not think those two sentences cancel each other out. Let me start with what is not arguable. The world is stunning. The light on the water at six in the morning is worth the price on its own, and I say that as somebody who normally nitpicks about frame rates. Whereas most survival games give you a grey box and call it an island, this one gives you a coastline you want to photograph. The sound design deserves the same praise. Now the other side, and admittedly I waited two years for this game, so take the disappointment with that in mind. The crafting menus are clunky in a way that a patch cannot fix, because the problem is the design and not the code. The side missions are repetitive after the first ten hours. Fetch this, carry that, come back. And the ending falls flat, no matter how carefully the rest of the story is built. So what is the verdict. On balance I would still tell you to buy it, and I would tell you to buy it on sale. The world makes up for the menus, although it does not make up for the ending, and the drawbacks are real even though none of them stopped me playing. If you want a story that pays you back at the end, this is not your game. If you want a place you actually miss when you close the laptop, it is, and that merit is not a small one.

First, say what the thing was trying to do, because a review that judges a game for not being a different game tells the reader nothing at all. Then give the strongest praise you honestly have, and give it before any complaint, since praise that arrives after the criticism always sounds like an apology. After that, name the drawback in one sentence and attach it to the praise with a concessive clause, so the reader sees the two weighed against each other instead of simply listed. Next, admit the part where you might be unfair, because somebody who waited two years for a game is not a neutral judge and the reader deserves to know that. Finally, give the verdict and say who it is for, so that a reader with completely different taste from yours can still use your review.
